clinicalPearls: A sex cord-stromal tumour of the testicular interstitial (Leydig) cells, and rarely of the ovarian hilus cells, that is often hormonally active

In boys it typically secretes testosterone autonomously, producing gonadotropin-independent precocious pseudopuberty with virilisation and, characteristically, a unilateral testicular enlargement or nodule
Because the androgen production is independent of the pituitary, gonadotropins are suppressed and the GnRH stimulation test remains prepubertal, distinguishing it from central precocious puberty
Some tumours also aromatise androgens to oestrogens and can cause gynaecomastia
The classic clue in a boy is asymmetric testicular enlargement disproportionate to the degree of virilisation, prompting scrotal examination and ultrasound

It must be distinguished from Leydig cell hyperplasia (for example due to chronic hCG or LH-receptor stimulation, or the testicular adrenal rest tissue of poorly controlled congenital adrenal hyperplasia) and from familial testotoxicosis
Most childhood Leydig cell tumours are benign, and testis-sparing surgery is often possible, with orchidectomy reserved for larger or suspicious lesions
reference.pathophysiology: A Leydig cell tumour arises from the testosterone-producing interstitial cells of the testis (or the analogous hilus cells of the ovary) and commonly retains steroidogenic activity, secreting androgens autonomously and sometimes aromatising them to oestrogens. The resulting sex-steroid excess is independent of pituitary gonadotropin drive, so the axis is suppressed and the clinical picture is one of precocious pseudopuberty rather than true, centrally mediated puberty. In boys this manifests as virilisation with an enlarged or nodular testis, whereas oestrogen production can cause gynaecomastia. The principal differential considerations are conditions that expand or stimulate Leydig cells without a true neoplasm, such as hyperplasia from chronic gonadotropin or LH-receptor stimulation, testicular adrenal rest tumours in congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and the activating LH-receptor disorder of familial testotoxicosis.
additionalDifferentials: Familial male-limited precocious puberty (testotoxicosis) from an activating LHCGR mutation
Leydig cell hyperplasia from chronic hCG or LH-receptor stimulation
Testicular adrenal rest tumour in congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Other sex cord-stromal or germ cell tumours of the testis
additionalInvestigations: Serum testosterone (and oestradiol where gynaecomastia is present) with basal LH and FSH (suppressed)
GnRH (LHRH) stimulation test demonstrating a prepubertal, suppressed response
Scrotal ultrasound to identify and characterise a testicular mass
Adrenal androgen profile including 17-hydroxyprogesterone to exclude congenital adrenal hyperplasia and rest tumours
Beta-hCG measurement to exclude an hCG-driven process
Histological examination of the resected lesion to confirm the diagnosis and assess for atypical features
redFlags: A distinct testicular mass or asymmetric enlargement in a boy with signs of androgen excess
Histological features suggesting malignancy (more common in adults than children), such as large size, necrosis, or vascular invasion
Rapidly progressive virilisation with markedly elevated testosterone
Persistence or recurrence of hormonal signs after surgery, suggesting residual or recurrent tumour
reference.prognosis: The great majority of Leydig cell tumours in childhood are benign, and removal (often testis-sparing) reverses the hormonal effects with an excellent outcome; malignant behaviour is uncommon in children but requires more extensive surgery and surveillance when present.
pitfalls: Mistaking the tumour for familial testotoxicosis or Leydig cell hyperplasia and thereby missing a resectable mass
Failing to examine and image the testes in a boy with gonadotropin-independent precocity
Overlooking testicular adrenal rest tissue of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which mimics a tumour but responds to glucocorticoid control
Performing orchidectomy when testis-sparing surgery would suffice for a benign lesion
Not confirming gonadotropin independence with a stimulation test before attributing signs to a central cause
management: Testis-sparing surgical excision (enucleation) as the definitive treatment, reversing the sex-steroid excess
Radical inguinal orchidectomy where organ preservation is not feasible or malignancy is suspected
Histological confirmation with assessment for atypical or malignant features
Distinguish preoperatively from Leydig cell hyperplasia, testicular adrenal rest tumours and familial testotoxicosis
Monitor resolution of virilisation or gynaecomastia and recovery of the suppressed gonadotropin axis
Assessment and management of accelerated bone age and predicted final height
Paediatric endocrinology and urology multidisciplinary care with postoperative surveillance
